question: A 12-year-old girl comes to the clinic with a grossly enlarged abdomen. She has a history of frequent episodes of weakness, sweating, and pallor that are eliminated by eating. Her development has been slow. She started to walk unassisted at 2 years and was not performing well at school. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg, heart rate of 80/min, and temperature of 36.9°C (98.4℉). On physical examination, the liver is enlarged, firm, and palpable up to the pelvis. The spleen and kidney are not palpable. Laboratory investigation reveals low blood glucose and pH with high lactate, triglycerides, ketones, and free fatty acids. The liver biopsy revealed high glycogen content. Hepatic glycogen structure was normal. The enzyme assay performed on the biopsy tissue revealed very low glucose-6-phosphatase levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Low blood glucose, high lactate, triglycerides, ketones, and free fatty acids" -> "Impaired glucose metabolism" -> "High glycogen content in the liver" -> "Normal hepatic glycogen structure" -> "Very low glucose-6-phosphatase levels" -> "Von-Gierke's disease" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Enlarged abdomen, slow development, weakness, sweating, pallor relieved by eating" -> "Low blood glucose, high lactate, triglycerides, ketones, and free fatty acids" -> "Impaired glucose metabolism" -> "High glycogen content in the liver" -> "Very low glucose-6-phosphatase levels" -> "Von-Gierke's disease" -> 90%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation of low blood glucose, high lactate, triglycerides, ketones, and free fatty acids, along with very low glucose-6-phosphatase levels and high glycogen content in the liver, is most indicative of Von-Gierke's disease. The symptoms of an enlarged abdomen, slow development, weakness, sweating, and pallor relieved by eating further support this diagnosis. The evidence paths do not provide additional relevant information for this case.
